newsitem.title: USA: Oil cos settle dispute over contaminated Brent oil.
newsitem.headline: Oil cos settle dispute over contaminated Brent oil.

text.p: Three oil companies have settled a dispute surrounding contaminated Brent crude oil that was delivered against the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) May crude contract, according to sources involved.

Northridge Energy Marketing Corp, a subsidiary of TrasnCanada Pipelines Ltd, agreed to pay 25-50 cents per barrel (bpd) in a private settlement with Shell Oil Co and Sinclair Oil Corp as part of an alternative delivery procedure (ADP) outside the exchange, the sources said.

A 500,000-barrel cargo of Brent that Northridge delivered against the May contract was found to have an unusually high 0.45 to 0.50 percent sulfur content, compared with the official NYMEX specification of 0.42 percent, the sources said.

"There is no question that the crude got contaminated during transit in Seaway," one of the sources said, referring to the pipeline run by Atlantic Richfield Co that goes from the Gulf Coast to the delivery hub at Cushing, Oklahoma.
ARCO officials were not immediately available to comment.
The delivery was part of a record 2.73 million total foreign barrels that were delivered against the May light sweet crude contract.
Most of the foreign deliveries were Bonny Light crude, part of which was also found to fall below official specifications, the source said.
Several batches of the Nigerian crude were found to have an API gravity of 34 degrees rather than the expected 36 degrees, sources said.

Sources familiar with the Bonny Light, which was delivered by Vitol S.A. Inc and ARCO, said a private deal was in the process of being hammered out to compensate the companies that received it, including Sinclair and Shell.
The new pattern of sharply rising foreign deliveries against the futures contract has led several large oil companies to cut back paper trading in favor of the more predictable cash market.
NYMEX officials held an unofficial meeting with market participants in Houston last Thursday to discuss the foreign deliveries, sources said.

Several traders for large oil companies say the NYMEX should cut the prices paid to sellers in order to discourage alternative deliveries and one suggested the NYMEX eliminate foreign deliveries altogether: "To put it on the list to force someone to take it is disruptive," the trader said.

But NYMEX has plans to increase the foreign exposure element of its contract. The July contract will allow delivery of Colombian Cusiana crude, joining the other foreign deliverable grades Bonny Light, Brent, Forties and Oseberg.
A NYMEX spokesperson said the exchange would change the contract if enough of its members demanded it.

"Our whole contract is designed to provide maximum flexibility and we continue to maintain that flexibility in consultation with the industry through our advisory committee. If a majority of the industry was in concert to makes changes, they would be reflected in the contract," the spokesperson said.
